div.p: The empire, which for long had been unsettled and, as it were, adrift, through the revolt and cutting off of three emperors, was at length taken in hand and firmly established by the Flavian family; an obscure family, it is true, and without portrait-masks, but yet one of which the commonwealth had no reason to be ashamed, though all agree that Domitian deserved the penalty he paid for avarice and cruelty.

Titus Flavius Petro, a townsman of Reate, who served as a centurion or a re-enlisted veteran on the side of Pompey in the civil war, fled from the battle of Pharsalus and betook himself home, where, having at last obtained a pardon and discharge, he carried on the business of a collector of moneys at bankers' sales. His son, surnamed Sabinus, of no military service (though some say that he was a centurion of the first rank, and others that while he was in command of a company he was invalided out of the army), farmed the state-tax of a fortieth in Asia; and there were in existence till later days statues set up to him by the cities in that province, with the inscription in Greek: "To an honest tax-farmer."

After this he became a money-lender among the Helvetii, and died there, leaving behind him his wife Vespasia Polla and two children by her, of whom the elder, Sabinus, rose to the rank of prefect of the city, and the younger, Vespasian, even to that of emperor. Polla, born of a good family at Nursia, had as father Vespasius Pollio, thrice tribune of the soldiers and prefect of the camp, and her brother was a senator of praetorian rank. There is moreover to this day on the top of a hill, at the sixth milestone from Nursia on the road to Spoletium, a place called Vespasiae, where many monuments of the Vespasii are to be seen, a striking proof of the lustre and antiquity of that family.

I would not deny that some have put about a story that the father of Petro came from the region beyond the Po and was a contractor for farmlabourers, who regularly cross each year from Umbria into the Sabine territory to till the fields; but that he settled in the town of Reate, where he took to himself a wife. I, for my part, have found no evidence whatever of this, even after full and diligent inquiry.

Vespasian was born in the Sabine country beyond Reate in a little village called Falacrina, on the evening of the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Quintus Sulpicius Camerinus and Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus, five years before the death of Augustus; and he was brought up under Tertulla, his grandmother on the father's side, on her property at Cosa. Wherefore, even after he became emperor, he used regularly to visit the place of his infancy, the villa being kept unchanged as it had been in former days, that his eyes might miss nothing of the familiar sight; and he cherished so devotedly the memory of his grandmother, that on solemn and festal days he continued to drink from a small silver cup which once was hers.

After assuming the garb of manhood he for long avoided the broad-striped senatorial tunic, though his brother had obtained it; nor could he be constrained by anyone but his mother to sue for it at last. She in the end forced his consent more by taunts than by entreaties and motherly authority, since again and again she slightingly called him his brother's lackey.

He served as military tribune in Thrace; as quaestor he received by lot the province of Crete and Cyrene; he was a candidate for the aedileship and soon after for the praetorship, but was once rejected for the former and then with difficulty secured it, coming sixth on the list, while the latter he gained when first he stood, being returned among the foremost. In his praetorship, in order to court in every way the favour of Gaius, who was at variance with the senate, he demanded special games to celebrate the emperor's victory in Germany, and moved in the senate that the punishment of the conspirators against him should be increased by casting forth their bodies unburied. He also returned thanks to him in presence of that most honourable order for deigning to grant him the honour of inviting him to dine.

In the meantime he took to wife Flavia Domitilla, formerly the mistress of Statilius Capella, a Roman knight of Sabrata in Africa, a woman who at first had only Latin rights, but afterwards was declared free-born and a Roman citizen by the Court of Recoverers on the claim of her father Flavius Liberalis, a native of Ferentium and merely a quaestor's clerk. By her he had as children Titus, Domitian, and Domitilla. He outlived his wife and daughter, and lost them both while still in a private station. After the death of his wife he brought back to cohabit with him Caenis, the freedwoman and secretary of Antonia, and formerly a favourite of his; and even after he became emperor he gave her almost the position of a lawful wife.

In the reign of Claudius he was sent, through the influence of Narcissus, to command a legion in Germany; from there he was transferred to Britain, and fought thirty battles with the enemy. He subdued two of the strongest tribes, more than twenty towns, and the isle of Vectis off the coast of Britain, partly under the leadership of Aulus Plautius, the consular governor, and partly under that of Claudius himself.

For these achievements he received the insignia of a triumph, and shortly afterwards two priestly offices, as well as the consulship, which he held for the last two months of the year. The period which intervened before his proconsulship he passed in quietude and retirement, through fear of Agrippina, who still had great influence with her son and hated bitterly any friend of Narcissus, even after Narcissus was dead.

After this he obtained by lot the province of Africa, which he governed with singular integrity and not without great honour, except that in an outbreak at Hadrumetum turnips were flung at him. It is certain that he returned to Rome none the richer, for his credit was so nearly ruined that he had to mortgage all his lands to his brother, and he was driven by necessity to stoop to trafficking in mules to support his position; for which reason he was commonly called "The Muleteer." He is said, moreover, to have been convicted of extorting two hundred thousand sesterces from a young man for whom he had obtained the broad-striped senatorial tunic against the wishes of his father, and to have been severely reprimanded for it.

He was one of the suite of Nero on his tour through Greece, and gave most dire offence by frequently going out of the theatre while Nero was singing, or by falling asleep, if he remained. By reason of this he was excluded not merely from the intimacy of the emperor but even from his public receptions, and he withdrew into a small secluded town, where he lay hid and feared the worst, until a province with the command of an army was offered to him.

Throughout the whole East had spread an old and persistent belief that it was ordained by Fate that there should at this time come forth from Judaea men who were to be lords of the whole world. This was a prediction concerning a Roman emperor, as the event afterwards showed, but the Jews took it to themselves and rose in revolt, and after slaying their governor, they further put to flight the consular commander of Syria, when he came to his support, and carried off one of his eagles. As the suppression of this revolt required a larger army and an enterprising general, yet such a one as could be safely entrusted with so great a command, Vespasian was chosen above all others, as a man of tried activity and one who by reason of the obscurity of his family and name was in no wise to be feared.

Accordingly there were added to the forces in Judaea two legions, eight squadrons, and ten cohorts. took his elder son as one of his lieutenants, and as soon as he reached his province he attracted the attention of the adjoining provinces also by reforming immediately the discipline of the camp and by engaging in one or two battles with such determination, that in the assault of a fortress he was wounded on the knee by the cast of a stone and received a number of arrows in his shield. He

After the death of Nero and Galba, when Otho and Vitellius were struggling for sovereignty, he came to have a great hope of empire, a hope which he had long since conceived by reason of the following portents.

On the suburban estate of the Flavii there stood an old oak, sacred to Mars, which at the three childbirths of Vespasia suddenly put forth separate boughs from the stock, undoubted signs of the future destiny of each child. The first bough was slender and quickly withered up, and so the daughter then born did not live through a single year; the second was very sturdy and long, presaging great good fortune; but the third had the likeness of a tree. Wherefore their father Sabinus, as the story goes, being further encouraged by an inspection of entrails, reported to his own mother that a grandson had been born to her who would be a Caesar; but she merely burst out laughing, marvelling that her son should be already doting, while she was still possessed of all her wits.

Afterwards in his aedileship, when Gaius Caesar, enraged that no care was taken by the aedile to have the streets swept clean, ordered him to be covered with mud, which the soldiers heaped in the bosom of his official gown, some interpreted this as a sign that one day the commonwealth, being trampled under foot and left neglected in some civil disorder, would come under his protection and, as it were, into his lap.

Once when he was lunching, a strange dog brought in a human hand from the cross-roads and dropped it beneath the table. Again, when he was dining, a ploughing ox shook off the yoke, burst into the dining-room, scattered the servants in flight, and fell down, as if suddenly weary, at the feet of Vespasian as he lay upon his couch, and bowed its neck to the ground. A cypress-tree, also, on his grandfather's land was torn up by the roots and laid flat without any violent storm, and the very next day rose up again greener and stronger than before.

Furthermore he dreamt in Achaea that good fortune would begin for him and his, when one of Nero's teeth was drawn; and it happened that on the following day a surgeon came out into the hall and showed him a tooth of Nero's newly drawn.

In Judaea, when he consulted the oracle of the god Carmel, the lots were so assuring as to promise him that whatever he was thinking upon or turning over in his mind, however great it might be, would come to fulfilment; and when Josephus, one of the captives of noble birth, was being put in chains, he most confidently asserted that he would shortly be released by the same man, who by that time, however, would be emperor.

From the city also presages were reported to him: that Nero at the close of his days was bidden by a dream to take the sacred car of Jupiter Optimus Maximus from its shrine and conduct it to the house of Vespasian, and from there to the Circus; that not long afterwards, when Galba was going to the election for his second consulship, the statue of the Deified Julius turned of itself towards the East; and that on the field of Betriacum, before battle was joined, two eagles engaged in sight of all, and when one of them was vanquished, a third came up from the rising of the sun and drove the victor off.
However he attempted nothing, though his friends were most ready and even urgent, until he was stirred to activity by the chance support of some who were unknown to him and at a distance.

Two thousand men from each of the three legions of the army in Moesia had been sent to the aid of Otho, and had started on their march when news came that Otho had been defeated and had laid violent hands upon himself; nevertheless they kept on as far as Aquileia, placing little reliance on the report. There, owing to the favourable opportunity and the lack of discipline, they indulged in every form of outrage and pillage; then, fearing that if they returned they would have to render an account and submit to punishment, they conceived the idea of choosing and creating an emperor, feeling that they were no whit inferior to the army in Spain which had appointed Galba, the praetorian guard which had appointed Otho, or the army in Germany which had appointed Vitellius.

Accordingly the names of all the consular governors at that time in any province were put forward for consideration, and since the rest met with disapproval for one reason or another, while some of the Third legion, which shortly before Nero's death had been transferred from Syria to Moesia, greatly extolled Vespasian, all agreed to him and forthwith inscribed his name on every standard. For the time, however, the scheme was checked, and the contingents were recalled to their allegiance for a little while. But when the news of this proceeding had spread abroad, Tiberius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, was the first to swear his legions to fealty to Vespasian on the Kalends of July, the day which ever afterwards was observed as the day of his accession; after them the army in Judaea took the oath of allegiance to Vespasian in person on the fifth day before the Ides of July.

These undertakings were greatly furthered by the circulation of a copy of a letter, genuine or forged, from the late emperor Otho to Vespasian, charging him, as a last solemn charge, to avenge his death, and hoping that he would come to the succour of the commonwealth; also, by the spreading of a report that Vitellius intended after his victory to change the winter-quarters of the legions and to transfer those in Germany to a safer and less arduous service in the East; furthermore, by the support given by Licinius Mucianus, one of the governors of provinces, and by Vologaesus of Parthia, one of the kings. The former, laying aside the animosity which up to that time he was clearly cherishing through jealousy, promised the army in Syria, and the latter forty thousand archers.

So having undertaken a civil war and sent forward generals and forces into Italy, he passed over in the meantime to Alexandria, to take possession of the key-positions of Egypt. There he ordered that all others be excluded and entered alone the temple of Serapis, to consult the auspices concerning the fixity of his empire, and when after many offerings to propitiate the god he at length turned about, he thought he saw his freedman Basilides holding out to him vervain and garlands and sacrificial cakes, as is the custom in that place; and yet it was known to all that no one had allowed Basilides to enter, and that for some time past he scarce could walk through stiffened sinews, and was moreover far away. And immediately letters arrived with the tidings that the troops of Vitellius had been routed at Cremona, and Vitellius himself slain at Rome.

Authority and, so to speak, sacred majesty were lacking as yet in an emperor who was unexpected and still newly appointed; but these also were now added to him. A man of the common people who was bereft of sight, and another who was lame, came both together to him as he sat upon the tribunal, craving the help for their infirmities which Serapis had shown them in a dream; for the god had assured them that Vespasian would restore sight to the one by spitting upon his eyes, and make strong the leg of the other, if he would but deign to touch it with his heel.

Though at first he had but little belief that the thing could in any way succeed, and so would not even venture to put it to the test, at last he was encouraged by his friends and essayed both cures before the assembled people, and not without success. About the same time at Tegea in Arcadia, through the promptings of some soothsayers, vases of antique workmanship were dug out of consecrated ground, and on them was an image like to Vespasian.

Such was the man, and so great the reputation with which he returned to Rome. After celebrating a triumph over the Jews, he added eight consulships to his former one; he also assumed the censorship, and during the whole period of his rule he made it his chief concern first to establish the commonwealth, which was wellnigh ruined and tottering to its fall, and then to beautify it as well.

The soldiers, part of them self-confident through victory, and part chafing at the humiliation of defeat, had gone every length in license and audacity; the provinces, also, and the free cities, as well as some of the vassal kingdoms, were disordered by internal turmoil. Accordingly he discharged a great many of the soldiers of Vitellius, and chastised many more; and so far was he from granting any special indulgence to the sharers of his victory, that it was late before he even paid the bounties which were their lawful due.

To let pass no opportunity of reforming military discipline, when a youth reeking with perfume came to return thanks to him for getting a cavalry commission, he drew back his head in disgust, rebuking him with the crushing words: "I had rather you smelt of garlic," and he recalled his appointment. When the marines who journey on foot by turns from Ostia and Puteoli to Rome petitioned to have some allowance made them under the name of “shoe-money," he was not content with sending them away without an answer, but ordered them for the future to run without shoes; and so they have done ever since.

He reduced to the form of provinces Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, and Samos, depriving them of their freedom, and likewise Cilicia the Rough and Commagene, which up to that time had been under the sway of kings. He assigned additional legions to Cappadocia on account of the constant inroads of the barbarians, and set over it a consular governor instead of a Roman knight.

As the city was unsightly from earlier fires and fallen buildings, he gave permission to anyone to take possession of the vacant sites and build upon them, if the owners were slow in doing so. It was he who set about the rebuilding of the Capitol, and he was the first to put his hand to clearing away the rubbish, even carrying some of it off on his own shoulders. Also he took upon himself the restoration of the three thousand bronze tablets which had been burnt with the temple, searching everywhere for copies of them: right glorious and right ancient records of the State, containing almost from the foundation of the city the decrees of the senate and ordinances of the people concerning alliances, treaties, and privileges granted to any.

He also carried out new works: a temple of Peace adjoining the Forum, and a temple of the Deified Claudius on the Caelian mount, which was begun, it is true, by Agrippina, but destroyed almost from the foundations by Nero; also an amphitheatre in the centre of the city, on learning that Augustus intended the same.

The two most honourable orders, depleted by manifold massacres and debased by years of neglect, he purged and recruited by holding a revision both of senators and knights, removing the most unworthy of them, and admitting the most illustrious of the Italians and provincials. And to let it be known that the two orders differed not so much in their prerogatives as in their position, on the occasion of a brawl between a senator and a Roman knight he gave it out as his decision: "Insults ought not to be used towards senators, but to return their insults is proper for any citizen and legally permissible."

The lists of lawsuits had grown to an abnormal size in every court, since the older ones still remained undecided through the interruption of judicial hearings, and new ones were being constantly added as a result of the disordered state of the times. He therefore chose by lot commissioners to provide for the restoration of property seized during the wars, and to exercise an extraordinary jurisdiction in deciding, and at the same time reducing to the smallest number, cases in the Hundred Judges' court, since it looked as if the lifetime of the litigants would hardly suffice for getting through these in the ordinary course.

Profligacy and prodigality had become rampant with none to check them, and so, on his motion, the senate decreed that a woman who formed a union with the bondman of another person should herself be accounted a bondwoman; also that money-lenders should at no time have the legal right of recovering advances to sons in tutelage, such restriction to hold good even after the father's death.

In all other matters, from the very beginning of his reign until the end, he was unpretentious and undespotic, never making any effort to conceal his former mean estate, but often glorying in it. Indeed, when some tried to trace back the origin of the Flavian family to the founders of Reate and the comrade of Hercules whose memorial still stands on the Salarian Way, he actually laughed at them. So utterly undesirous was he of к 2 adventitious decorations, that on the day of his triumph, wearied out by the slowness and tediousness of the procession, he could not keep from observing: "It is a proper punishment for being so silly in my old age as to hanker after a triumph, as if it were either due to my ancestors, or had ever been among my hopes." He did not accept even the tribunician power or the title of Father of his Country till late in his reign. As for the custom of searching those who came to pay their respects, he had dropped that before the civil war was ended.

The outspokenness of his friends, the innuendoes of pleaders, and the petulance of philosophers he endured with the greatest forbearance. When Licinius Mucianus, a notorious degenerate, presumed on his services to be wanting in respect to him, he never could bring himself to speak harshly in return except privately, and then merely to the extent of winding up a complaint to a common friend with the words "I at least am a man." When Salvius Liberalis in defending a wealthy client ventured to say: "What matters it to Caesar if Hipparchus has a hundred million sesterces?'' he personally commended him. When Demetrius the Cynic, after being sentenced to banishment, met him on a journey and did not deign either to rise up or to salute him, but even snarled out some abuse, he contented himself with calling him "dog."

So little did he remember or avenge affronts or animosities that he made a splendid match for the daughter of his enemy Vitellius, and further furnished her with a dowry and equipment. When he was in a panic at being forbidden the court in Nero's reign and kept asking what he was to do or where he was to go, one of the ushers thrusting him out ordered him to "go to Pest"; but when this same man afterwards craved his pardon, Vespasian confined his wrath to words, and those about the same in number and to the same effect. For so far was he from being moved by any suspicion or fear to seek the destruction of anyone, that when his friends warned him to beware of Mettius Pompusianus, because he was generally believed to have a horoscope predicting empire, he went the length of making him consul, guaranteeing that one day he would be mindful of this favour.

It would be hard to find a case of an innocent person being punished in his reign, unless it were when he was absent and knew nothing of it, or at least against his will and through his being misinformed. Although Helvidius Priscus had been the only person to greet him on his return from Syria by his private name of "Vespasian," and as praetor had passed him over without honour and mention in all his edicts, he showed no wrath until Helvidius by most insolent rejoinders had almost reduced him to the level of a common citizen. Yet even in his case, though he ordered first his banishment and then his death, he would have given much to save his life by any possible means, and he sent messengers to recall the executioners; and he would have saved him, had it not been for a false report that he had already been despatched. In short, he never rejoiced at the violent death of anyone, and even wept and sighed at punishments, however just.

The only thing for which he can reasonably be blamed was a fondness for money. For not content with having renewed the taxes dropped under Galba, with having added others new and onerous, with having increased the tribute of the provinces, actually doubling it in some instances, he also engaged openly in trafficking which would disgrace even a private citizen, buying up certain commodities merely in order to retail them afterwards at a profit.

He did not scruple even to sell political offices to candidates, or acquittals to those under prosecution, whether innocent or guilty. Moreover, he is believed to have made a practice of deliberately promoting the most rapacious of his procurators to higher posts, so that they might be the richer when he condemned them presently; for it was said that he used them like sponges, soaking them, as it were, when they were dry and squeezing them when they were wet.

Some say that he was naturally most avaricious, and that this was cast in his teeth by an aged herdsman of his, who, on his refusal to grant without payment the freedom for which he had humbly petitioned him when he came to the throne, exclaimed: "The fox may change his fur, but not his nature." There are those on the contrary who think that he was driven to spoil and to plunder by necessity through the utter depletion of the public exchequer and his private treasury, to which he himself bore witness at the very beginning of his reign by his pronouncement that forty thousand million sesterces were needful to set the State upright again. And this seems nearer to the truth, for even his ill-gotten gains he employed to excellent purpose.

He showed himself most generous to every class, making up the property qualification requisite for senators, supporting impoverished ex-consuls by yearly grants of five hundred thousand sesterces, and restoring in a more splendid form a great number of cities throughout the world, which had been laid in ruins by earthquake or by fire.

He gave the greatest encouragement to literary talent and the arts. He was the first to establish for Latin and Greek professors of rhetoric an annual salary of one hundred thousand sesterces from his own coffers. On eminent poets as well as on artists, such as the restorers of the Coan Venus and the Colossus, he bestowed notable bounties and generous gifts. To an engineer, who offered to convey some lofty columns up to the Capitol at a small expense, he gave no mean reward for his device, but declined his services with the remark: “You must allow me to feed my poor commons."

At the plays with which he dedicated the reconstructed stage in the theatre of Marcellus he revived the old recitals of artistes. To Apelles, the tragedian, he gave four hundred thousand sesterces; to Terpnus and Diodorus, the lyre-players, two hundred thousand each; to others one hundred thousand; to those who received least forty thousand; besides which he gave a great number of golden crowns. He also entertained continually, generally at formal banquets sumptuously furnished, to help the market-vendors. He gave table-presents to the women upon the Kalends of March each year, as he did to the men at the Saturnalia. And yet with all this he could not rid himself of his former ill-repute for avarice.

The Alexandrians persisted in calling him Cybiosactes ("Chopped-fish Huckster'"), the surname of one of their own kings who was most discreditably mean. Even at his funeral, Favor, the principal mime, wearing a mask of the emperor and mimicking, as the custom is, his deeds and words during his lifetime, asked loudly of the procurators what the funeral with its procession would cost, and when he heard "Ten million sesterces," he cried: "Give me a hundred thousand for myself and you may throw me into the Tiber if you like."

In build he was well-proportioned, with compact sturdy limbs, and the expression of one who was straining hard, touching which a noted wit, when the emperor asked him to say something clever about him too, observed rather neatly: "I will do so, when you have done easing yourself." He enjoyed the best of health, though he never did more to preserve it than to rub his throat and the other parts of his body a regular number of times in the ball-court, and to interpose one day's fasting every month.

The mode of life which he observed was very much as follows. When emperor, he always woke unusually early and even before daybreak; then, after reading through his letters and the summary reports of all the officials, he admitted his friends, and while he was receiving their greetings, he put on his shoes and dressed himself. After disposing of any business that came before him, he had leisure for a drive and then for a siesta, reclining with one of his concubines, of whom he had appointed a great number in the place of Caenis on her death. From his private apartment he passed into the bath and thence to the dining-room; and it is said that at no time was he more gracious or indulgent, and his household eagerly seized these brief opportunities to prefer their requests.

Moreover at dinner, and indeed at all other times, he was most affable, and he settled many matters with a jest; for he had a great amount of humour, though of such a vulgar and scurrilous kind that he did not even refrain from the most ribald expressions. Yet there are still current some very witty remarks of his, and among them the following. Being once reminded by Mestrius Florus, an ex-consul, that the proper pronunciation was plaustra and not plostra, he greeted him next day as "Flaurus." When he was stormed by the advances of a certain lady who protested that she was dying of love for him, he admitted her to his couch, and gave her four hundred thousand sesterces as a reward for her favours; and when his steward raised the question how he wished this sum to be entered in his accounts, he replied: "To an infatuation for Vespasian."

He also quoted Greek verses quite appositely, as in the case of a man tall of stature, who had enormous parts: "Mighty his stride, and his long-shadowed spear is a-waving," and in the case of the freedman Cerylus, who was very wealthy, and in order to evade the claims of the imperial purse at death, had begun to pass himself off as free-born and changed his name to Laches: "O Laches, Laches, when death comes to thee, Thy name, as erstwhile, Cerylus shall be." Chiefly, however, he affected wit in the matter of his shameful gains, seeking to efface the odium thereof by some merry quip, and to turn it into a jest.

When one of his favourite court-attendants sought of him a stewardship for a pretended brother, he put him off and summoned the candidate himself, and after squeezing out of him the sum which he had promised his supporter, he appointed him without delay. Soon after, when the court-attendant put in a word again, he said: "Look out for another brother for yourself; the one you think is yours is mine." Once on a journey suspecting that the muleteer had jumped down to shoe the mules merely with the object of delaying and giving a litigant time to approach the emperor, he asked him how much he was getting for the shoeing, and stipulated for a part of the profit.

When his son Titus found fault with him for devising a revenue from urine, he held the money from the first payment to his son's nostrils and asked him was he offended with the smell; when Titus answered "No," he said: "And yet it comes from urine." When deputies announced that a colossal statue of no ordinary cost had been decreed him at the public charge, he bade them set it up then and there, showing the hollow of his hand and saying: "The base is ready."

Not even the apprehension and immediate peril of death could keep him from jesting. For when, among other prodigies, the Mausoleum (of the Caesars) suddenly opened and a comet (long-haired star) appeared in the heavens, he declared that the former referred to Junia Calvina of the family of Augustus, and the latter to the king of the Parthians, who wore long hair; also at the first attack of his last illness he said: "Woe is me! I suppose I am becoming a god."

In his ninth consulship he was attacked by a slight disorder while in Campania, and returning at once to the city, he went from there to Cutiliae and the country about Reate, where he used to pass the summer every year. There, in addition to his increasing malady, he did harm to his intestines by a too frequent use of the cold spring, but nevertheless continued to discharge his duties as emperor, and even gave audience to ambassadors as he lay in bed. Seized of a sudden by such a loosening of the bowels that he all but swooned, he said: "An emperor ought to die standing," and while he struggled to rise, he died in the hands of those who tried to help him up, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, at the age of sixty-nine years, seven months, and seven days.

All agree that he had such unvarying confidence in his own horoscope and in those of his sons, that even after the incessant conspiracies against him he had the boldness to assure the senate that either his sons would succeed him or no one would. It is said, moreover, that he once dreamt that he saw a balance hanging in the midst of the vestibule of his palace, with its beam in equipoise, and in the one scale of it stood Claudius and Nero, in the other himself and his sons. Nor did the event belie the vision, since both families reigned for the same number of years and the exact same space of time.
